name: Tawang Monpa
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Dondrup, Rinchin 1988. Handbook on Tawang Monpa Language. Itanagar: Directorate of Research; also Huang 1992 phonological analysis (tonal, per Wikipedia). Neither text loadable; Glottolog entry retired (= Dakpa).

sources.citation: Bodt, Timotheus A. 2023. East Bodish revisited. Bulletin of Tibetology 54(1): 49-212 (scanned text of the issue PDF).
sources.note: Comparative-historical; footnote p. 73 says the Dakpa varieties in Lu (1986, 2002) basically have a distinctive high vs. low register tone onset; grep for stress/accent/prosod- gives no relevant hit.

sources.citation: Tombleson, Anette Helgestad. 2022. Grammar sketch of Tawang Monpa. Himalayan Linguistics 21(2): 105-141. doi:10.5070/H921252709.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Sec. 2 Phonology (pp. 106-110); sec. 2.3 'Tone and vowel length' (p. 109-110): two-way high/low tone, contrastive only after sonorants, predictable after stops; author does not mark tone; the words stress/accent do not occur anywhere in the sketch.

sources.citation: van Driem, George. 2007. Dzala and Dakpa form a coherent subgroup within East Bodish, and some related thoughts. In R. Bielmeier & F. Haller (eds.), Linguistics of the Himalayas and beyond, 71-84. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
sources.note: pp. 75-76 'phonological impressionism': 'There may, however, be register tone similar to the binary distinction characteristic of Dzongkha'; preglottalised high-register syllables; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2006. Change Request 2006-034 (create [twm] Tawang Monpa, etc.). SIL International.
sources.note: Lexicostatistic percentages and naming only; no phonology.

sources.citation: Michailovsky, Boyd & Martine Mazaudon. 1994. Preliminary notes on the languages of the Bumthang group. In Per Kvaerne (ed.), Tibetan Studies (PIATS Fagernes 1992), vol. 2, 545-557. Oslo. HAL halshs-00259369.
sources.note: Phonology section (pp. 546-547) describes Kurtoep (two tonal registers); Dakpa figures only as comparative wordlist data (sec. 1.1 and cognate tables); nothing on Dakpa stress.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Takpa language' (accessed 2026-09-17), phonology section citing Huang Bufan (ed.) 1992 Zangmianyuzu yuyan cihui p. 634 for Cuona Monba.
sources.note: Tertiary: 'Monba is a tonal language, with four contour tones: 55, 53, 35, and 31.' Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Nishida, Tatsuo. 1988 [1989]. The mTsho-sna Monpa language of China and its place in the Tibeto-Burman family. In D. Bradley, E.J.A. Henderson & M. Mazaudon (eds.), Prosodic analysis and Asian linguistics: to honour R.K. Sprigg, 223-236. Pacific Linguistics C-104. doi:10.15144/PL-C104.223.
sources.note: Comparative, based on Sun et al. 1980 / Lu 1986 (Cuona Monpa, Mama and Wenlang dialects). pp. 231-233: syllable tones 53, 55, 35, 31 (Mama), high series after voiceless initials, low after voiced; disyllables tend to integrate into 55-53 and 35-53 tone patterns. No mention of stress or accent.

sources.citation: Hyslop, Gwendolyn & Karma Tshering. 2010. Preliminary notes on Dakpa (Tawang Monpa). In Stephen Morey & Mark Post (eds.), North East Indian Linguistics 2, 3-21. New Delhi: Cambridge University Press India / Foundation Books.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.access_detail: publisher DOI, paywalled; Harvard e-access not checked
sources.note: The only other modern first-hand sketch (19 pp.) with a phonology section by a specialist in East Bodish tone/prosody; most likely place for an explicit remark on stress or its absence in Dakpa.

sources.citation: Wangchu, Lhama. 2002. An introduction to the Tawang Monpa language. Itanagar: Directorate of Research, Government of Arunachal Pradesh. 96 pp.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.access_detail: print only, per the reader; access check: not located online or at Harvard
sources.note: Locally produced introduction to the Tawang variety itself; Directorate of Research guides usually open with a sound-system chapter that may comment on accent.

sources.citation: Lu Shaozun 陆绍尊. 1986. 错那门巴语简志 (Cuona Menbayu jianzhi). Beijing: Minzu chubanshe.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: Fullest phonology of the language (Mama dialect = Dakpa): initials, finals, four tones, syllable structure, sandhi; jianzhi volumes sometimes note 轻声/重音 in polysyllables.

sources.citation: Bodt, Timotheus A. 2012. The New Lamp clarifying the history, peoples, languages and traditions of Eastern Bhutan and Eastern Mon. Wageningen: Monpasang Publications.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: Contains short phonological sketches of Dakpa and neighbouring East Bodish languages by a fieldworker on the area (Dakpa phonology around p. 283 per earlier audit note); may state prosodic type.

sources.citation: Lu Shaozun 陆绍尊. 2002. 门巴语方言研究 (Menbayu fangyan yanjiu) [A study of Monpa dialects]. Beijing: Minzu chubanshe.

sources.note: Dialect monograph covering Mama, Dawang (Tawang), Wenlang and Bangxin varieties with full tonal transcription; would supersede the 1986 jianzhi on prosody and covers the Tawang variety proper.

sources.citation: Sun Hongkai 孙宏开, Lu Shaozun 陆绍尊, Zhang Jichuan 张济川 & Ouyang Jueya 欧阳觉亚. 1980. 门巴、珞巴、僜人的语言 (Menba, Luoba, Dengren de yuyan). Beijing: Zhongguo shehui kexue chubanshe.
